metaTitle: Best Generators for Well Pumps in 2026
metaDescription: Four generators that can start a residential well pump, compared on running watts, 240V capability, transfer switch readiness and fuel flexibility.
expertTake: The Westinghouse 6600 dual fuel is the pick for a typical half-horsepower to one-horsepower well pump because 5,300 running watts and a transfer-ready outlet give real starting headroom at a sensible size. The A-iPower 5000 is the value pick for a shallow 120V pump, and anyone with a deep 240V pump plus a whole house load should step up to the 13500 class.
introParagraphs: A well pump is one of the hardest loads a small generator will ever see. It is an induction motor that draws several times its running power for a fraction of a second on every start, and in a house with a pressure tank it starts again every time someone runs a tap.

Without the pump, a rural home has no water for drinking, flushing or washing, which is why this is a different buying exercise from backing up a fridge. The decision comes down to pump voltage, starting surge, and a safe way to connect the generator to the well circuit rather than a cord to the pump itself.

products.name: Westinghouse 6600W Dual Fuel Home Backup Generator
products.description:
Most residential well pumps are half to one horsepower and draw roughly a thousand watts while running, with a startup surge of three times that or more. A generator with 5,300 running watts and 6,600 peak watts has the headroom to handle that surge and still run a few other circuits. It is the size where a pump stops being a gamble and becomes a planned load.

What makes this Westinghouse suitable is the L14-30R transfer-ready outlet, which is a 120/240V twist-lock intended for a transfer switch or interlock inlet. A 240V submersible pump will only run through a proper connection like that, not through a household plug. Dual fuel adds a propane option with 4,800 running watts, and the included propane hose means you are not shopping for parts before the first outage.

Against the 13500 class, it is lighter and more fuel efficient for a pump-only load, and it avoids the idle burn of a big engine. Test the pump on the generator before an emergency, with the main breaker off and the transfer switch set correctly, and keep the oil topped up, since a pump may cycle on and off for hours while the engine runs. One wiring reality deserves a mention: the pump is only one part of the well circuit. The pressure switch, the control box on a three-wire submersible and any booster pump all share it, so confirm which breaker feeds the whole assembly before you wire the inlet.
products.bestFor: Typical home wells with a half to one horsepower pump and a modest house load.
pros: 5,300 running watts clears typical pump surge
L14-30R outlet suits a 240V transfer inlet
Ships with oil, hose and a tool kit
cons: Not enough for a deep pump plus central air
Propane mode drops usable running watts

products.name: Westinghouse 13500W Dual Fuel Home Backup Generator
products.description:
This is the right machine if the well pump is one of many loads, because it combines abundant surge capacity with a 9.5-gallon tank that carries a week of intermittent pump cycles. A deep submersible 240V pump with a one-horsepower motor starts easily on this much generator, and the headroom lets a fridge, a furnace blower and lights share the circuit.

Pairing it with the Westinghouse WATS200 automatic transfer switch means the well keeps running when the grid drops, even if you are away, which matters for a household with animals or a pump that feeds a pressure tank. The pressure lubrication system on the 500cc engine pushes oil to the bearings, a design better suited to long run times than splash lubrication.

The cost is size and fuel burn. Running a 13,500-watt machine for a pump that draws a thousand watts is inefficient, and the 6600 in this list does the job with less fuel. Check the oil often, keep the battery healthy for the electric start, and test the automatic switch each season. If you also keep a sump pump or a well-water treatment system, the 13500 can carry them at once, which is the practical argument for the larger size. Fuel logistics are the counterweight: one tank fill carries a long time at pump-only loads, so you may refuel less often than the quarter-load figure suggests. Keep the battery on a maintainer so the electric start and the automatic switch are ready when the grid drops.
products.bestFor: Homes that combine a deep well pump with fridges, heating and other circuits.
pros: Huge surge capacity for any residential pump
Pairs with an automatic transfer switch
cons: Burns more fuel than needed for a pump-only load

products.name: Westinghouse 13500W Tri-Fuel Home Backup Generator
products.description:
Rural homes with a well often have propane tanks or a natural gas line, and this version runs on either one. A buried propane tank can hold weeks of fuel, so a pump that cycles intermittently can run for days without anyone refilling a can. Natural gas, where available, takes refueling out of the picture.

The mechanical package matches the dual fuel 13500 with a 500cc pressure-lubricated engine and a 9.5-gallon gasoline tank, so you get gasoline as a fallback and an automatic transfer switch pairing for unattended use. A tri-fuel unit costs more, so it makes sense only if you have the gas supply to use it.

Ownership depends on the plumbing: have a licensed installer connect the gas line, run the unit monthly on the fuel you plan to use, and verify the regulator and hose connections. Do not plan to run a deep well pump through an extension cord, because a transfer inlet is the right way to connect it. A buried propane tank also gives you a clean fuel story for the rest of the house, since the same supply can feed a furnace or a range. Ask the installer to size the regulator and line for the generator draw at full load, not just the appliances already connected. Confirm the tank level gauge reads correctly before storm season.
products.bestFor: Rural homes with propane or natural gas supply and an automatic transfer plan.
pros: Runs on gasoline, propane or natural gas
Large surge reserve for deep pumps
cons: More expensive and heavier than needed for a pump alone

products.name: A-iPower 5000W Portable Generator with CO Sensor
products.description:
A 223cc engine with a cast iron sleeve and 4,000 running watts is a sound basis for a shallow 120V well pump, where the motor surge sits around two to three thousand watts. This is the budget way to keep a jet pump running without buying a home-backup-class machine.

The listing shows 5-20R household outlets and a CO shutdown sensor, but no 240V or transfer-ready outlet in the data we reviewed, so it is not the pick for a deep submersible 240V pump unless you confirm a 240V receptacle. Its 68 dB noise rating is conventional open-frame loudness, so place it well away from the house. Outlet flexibility and propane operation are what it surrenders to the Westinghouse 6600, in exchange for a lower price.

For ownership, the first thing to check is the pump nameplate, then the outlet match. Keep fresh fuel, change oil after the first break-in hours, and use a heavy-gauge cord rated for the pump's current if you are plugging a 120V pump directly. Consider a soft starter on the pump, which lowers the startup surge and lets a smaller generator cope. If the pump is a deep 240V model, skip this unit unless the manufacturer confirms a 240V outlet, because a surge at the wrong voltage simply will not start the motor. For a shallow well supplying a cabin or a garden, it is a solid and affordable match. Wire it through a properly sized cord and check that the voltage under load stays above 110 volts at the pump.
products.bestFor: Shallow 120V jet pumps and lighter well loads on a budget.
pros: 4,000 running watts handles a 120V well pump
223cc cast iron sleeve engine for durability
CO sensor shuts the engine down automatically
Lower price tier than the Westinghouse units
cons: No 240V or transfer outlet in the listing data

buyingCriteria.explanation: Shallow jet pumps often run on 120V, while deep submersible pumps usually need 240V. A generator without a 240V outlet cannot run a 240V pump no matter how many watts it has. The Westinghouse 6600 offers an L14-30R 120/240V transfer outlet, while the A-iPower 5000 data shows only 120V receptacles.

An induction pump motor can draw three to five times its running watts for a brief moment. A half-horsepower pump running near 900 watts can briefly demand 3,000 or more. The 5,300 running watts of the Westinghouse 6600 absorbs that spike while the 4,000 running watts of the A-iPower is closer to the limit.

A well pump is hardwired, so the safe method is a transfer switch or an interlock kit on the main panel. Extension cords to the pump are unsafe and often violate code. The Westinghouse units list transfer-ready outlets, and the 13500 pairs with an automatic switch.

A soft starter on the pump reduces startup current and can let a smaller generator succeed. It is a good upgrade if your generator is marginal. Check compatibility with the pump's motor type first. Most soft starters are sized by horsepower and voltage, so match them to the pump label.

A well pump on a pressure tank cycles intermittently, so fuel use is modest, but an outage can last days. Propane from a buried tank, supported by the Westinghouse dual fuel and tri-fuel units, beats storing gasoline for months.

Run the generator outdoors, far from the house, with the exhaust pointed away from windows and vents. The A-iPower 5000 includes a CO sensor shutdown, a useful backstop but not a substitute for proper placement.

specDecoder.meaning: Running watts are continuous output, peak is a few-second surge. A pump needs both.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Westinghouse 6600 offers 6,600 peak and 5,300 running watts, while the A-iPower 5000 offers 5,000 and 4,000.

specDecoder.meaning: A 120/240V 30 amp twist-lock outlet used for transfer switches and inlets.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Westinghouse 6600 and 13500 list transfer-ready outlets, which a 240V pump hookup needs.

specDecoder.meaning: The brief current draw when a motor starts, listed on the pump nameplate and the reason surge is so high.
specDecoder.watchFor: Multiply nameplate running amps by three to five to find a safe peak target before choosing between the 4,000-watt A-iPower and the 5,300-watt Westinghouse.

specDecoder.meaning: Dual fuel units list separate gasoline and propane ratings.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Westinghouse 6600 falls from 5,300 running watts on gasoline to 4,800 on propane.

specDecoder.meaning: Waveform distortion. Pumps tolerate it but pressure switches and controllers can be picky.
specDecoder.watchFor: None of the four lists a THD figure in the data we reviewed, so ask the seller before connecting a variable-speed pump controller.

howWeEvaluated.title: Surge capacity
howWeEvaluated.description: We matched peak and running watts to typical half to one horsepower pump startup surges. The Westinghouse 6600 and 13500 cleared with headroom. The A-iPower 5000 cleared shallow pumps only.

howWeEvaluated.title: Voltage and outlet match
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked whether each machine lists a 240V or transfer-ready outlet. The Westinghouse units did, the A-iPower listing did not. A 240V deep pump needs the proper outlet and a safe inlet.

howWeEvaluated.title: Fuel strategy
howWeEvaluated.description: We rewarded dual and tri-fuel designs for outages that stretch for days. Propane output on the 6600 is 4,800 running watts. A gasoline-only unit needs stored fuel.

howWeEvaluated.title: Safety features
howWeEvaluated.description: CO sensor shutdown, low-oil protection and transfer-ready connections were compared using the spec sheets. The A-iPower and Westinghouse units both emphasize CO protection.

howWeEvaluated.title: Efficiency for a pump load
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered that a large engine is wasteful for a thousand-watt pump. The 6600 hits the sweet spot, while the 13500 pair earns its place only when other loads share the circuit.

Deep 240V submersible, half to one hp

cards.label: Right-sized
cards.text: The Westinghouse 6600 and A-iPower 5000 match the pump's load without burning excess fuel. They cost less to buy and run, but leave less room if your needs grow.

cards.label: Oversized
cards.text: The Westinghouse 13500 dual and tri-fuel units handle any pump and extra circuits. They burn more fuel idling at light load and need more space.

howToChoose.note: Choose right-sized if the pump is the only critical load. Choose oversized if you want whole-house backup.

rows: Portable use at a cabin well

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Check the pump's nameplate for voltage, horsepower and amps, and check the wiring depth. Deep submersible pumps are 240V, so you need a 120/240V connection through a transfer switch or interlock. Look for a soft-start option on the pump controller.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Westinghouse 6600 is the smallest machine here with the transfer-ready outlet a 240V pump needs. The 13500 dual fuel and tri-fuel versions suit a deep pump that shares the circuit with other loads.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You rely on the well for livestock or for a household that cannot go without water, or you want automatic starts while away. The Westinghouse 13500 and tri-fuel versions earn the price.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You have a shallow 120V pump and short outages. The A-iPower 5000 handles that with a lower budget and simpler use.

maintenance.why: Start the pump from the generator with the main breaker off to confirm the generator can handle the surge. Find the weak point before an emergency.
A pump may cycle for hours and low-oil shutdown would stop your water. Add oil as needed.
Stale gasoline gums the carburetor, the top failure cause. Rotate fuel yearly.
Look for cracks and test fittings with soapy water. A leaking hose is a fire risk.

A waterlogged pressure tank makes the pump short-cycle and increases the number of starts. Fix it to reduce generator strain. A tank charged to the right pressure also protects the pump motor from rapid cycling.

faq.q: How big a generator do I need for a well pump?
faq.a: A half to one horsepower pump typically needs 3,000 to 5,000 starting watts, so a generator with 4,000 to 5,300 running watts is comfortable. Check the nameplate and multiply running amps by three to five. A pump that trips the generator on every start usually means the surge exceeds the peak rating, so add a soft starter or move up a size.

faq.q: Can a generator run a 240V submersible pump?
faq.a: Yes, but it needs a 240V output and a safe connection, such as a transfer switch or interlock. The Westinghouse 6600 and 13500 list transfer-ready outlets.

faq.q: Do I need a transfer switch?
faq.a: For a hardwired pump, yes. A transfer switch or interlock kit prevents backfeeding the grid and lets you power the pump circuit safely. A licensed electrician can install an interlock kit in a few hours, and the work usually requires a permit.

A soft starter reduces startup surge and can let a smaller generator succeed. It does not replace correct sizing, but it is a cost-effective upgrade. Match the soft starter to the pump horsepower and voltage listed on the nameplate.

faq.q: How much fuel will the pump use?
faq.a: A pump only runs when you draw water, so fuel use is modest compared with a refrigerator. Larger engines still burn fuel at idle, so right-size when you can.

faq.q: Can I use an extension cord to the pump?
faq.a: Only for a 120V pump with a short, heavy-gauge cord rated for the current. Deep 240V pumps should be connected through a transfer inlet. Never use a household extension cord for a long run to a pump house, because voltage drop can stop the motor from starting.
